paras: The attempted lynching of Hardy Clifford was an attempt or threat by indignant crowds to lynch Clifford, a Milwaukee gambler, at Racine, Wisconsin, in April 1882 after he shot and killed Capt. W. R. Pugh. Wire reports carried across the country predicted that he would be lynched that night, but Clifford stayed in jail under militia protection and was later convicted of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment. No report gives Clifford's race.

On Friday night, April 14, Pugh and Clifford had wagered $175 on a walking match at Belle City Hall between Higgie of Racine and Dammars of Chicago, which Higgie won. According to the Kenosha Telegraph, Clifford refused to let the stakeholder pay out and accused Pugh of having bought up the walkers, then went to the Huggins House. When Pugh led him by the coat toward the stairs to settle, Clifford drew a revolver; two shots went into the wall and floor and two struck Pugh, who died Saturday morning. A New York Sun dispatch instead said Clifford shot Pugh twice in the back and twice in the breast, and the Manitowoc Pilot put the bet at $50.
Pugh, captain of the schooner Rainbow, was described as wealthy, popular and well known on the Great Lakes, while Clifford was called a gambler of violent temper.

Clifford gave himself up to the officers and was lodged in jail. A Milwaukee dispatch of April 15 said that "Reports from Racine state that Clifford will be lynched to-night," and a fuller version added that Pugh, a Welshman, had countrymen in Milwaukee who sent a large delegation to Racine that evening to take part in the lynching. The Kenosha Telegraph wrote that the people were so indignant that "an attempt was made to lynch him," and that the militia was ordered out for his protection. The coverage does not describe what the attempt consisted of, and the Manitowoc Pilot reported only "some threats of lynching" before the indignation subsided.

For fear of "vengeance at the hands of Pugh's friends," Clifford was arraigned in the sheriff's residence next to the jail, where he pleaded not guilty. The excitement died away during Monday, and Pugh's funeral on Tuesday drew what the Telegraph called the largest crowd ever gathered in the city to honor a citizen.

Clifford's preliminary examination before Justice Snyder was postponed to May 3 at the request of the District Attorney. In December 1882 he was tried at Janesville, and the jury found him guilty of murder in the first degree; a motion for a new trial was made. The Superior Times reported that he was sentenced to the penitentiary for life. No arrests of anyone for the lynching attempt appear in the coverage.

The short Milwaukee wire ran on April 15 and 16 in papers from Rock Island and New York to Seattle, under heads such as "Fear of Violence" and "Killed by a Noted Gambler." These items treated the lynching as all but certain, and none carried a correction when it did not happen; one Sacramento digest even reversed the roles, saying Clifford had been killed by Pugh.

Wisconsin weeklies supplied the later detail. The Kenosha Telegraph called Clifford a "murderous villain" and the popular feeling "a righteous indignation," warning that he might yet meet a law "which an indlgnant and injured people make for themselves." The Manitowoc Pilot instead blamed the recent acquittal of another Milwaukee gambler for encouraging the shooting. None of the coverage mentions race.

Accounts differ on how far the mob went: the Kenosha Telegraph reported an attempt that required the militia, while the Manitowoc Pilot reported only threats that subsided. His first name also appears as Harvey, Harry and Hartley, and his age as 21 or 28.

bases: After Clifford shot Capt. W. R. Pugh, wire reports said he would be lynched and a Milwaukee delegation went to Racine to take part (A1, A10); the Kenosha Telegraph reported an attempt to lynch him in jail that the militia was ordered out to prevent (A13). Nothing in the coverage states Clifford's race.

Clifford was not killed: he remained in custody, was tried at Janesville and sentenced to life imprisonment (A13, A19, A20). The episode is at most an attempted or threatened lynching of a man whose race is never stated (A12, A13).

The shooting and the lynching threat are corroborated by several independent reports (A1, A3, A10, A11), but the Kenosha Telegraph says an attempt was made (A13) while the Manitowoc Pilot says there were only 'some threats' that subsided (A12).
